documents.abstract: Abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence has substantially changed the way academic writing can be taught, practiced, and assessed in higher education. This article examines the theoretical and pedagogical principles underlying AI-assisted academic writing instruction, with particular attention to learner agency, process-oriented writing, scaffolding, feedback, metacognition, academic integrity, and human–AI collaboration. The study adopts a theoretical-analytical methodology based on a review and synthesis of recent research on generative AI in education, academic writing pedagogy, and responsible technology use. The analysis shows that AI is most pedagogically valuable when it is used not as a substitute for student thinking, but as a scaffold that supports planning, drafting, revision, language development, and critical reflection. Effective AI-assisted writing instruction therefore requires a shift from product-oriented assessment toward process-oriented pedagogy, in which students make visible how ideas are generated, evaluated, revised, and verified. The article also argues that academic integrity should be addressed through transparent AI-use policies, source verification, disclosure, and the development of AI literacy rather than through prohibition alone. A pedagogically sound model of AI-assisted academic writing is thus based on human agency, iterative feedback, critical evaluation, ethical responsibility, and purposeful integration of digital tools into the writing process. Keywords: generative artificial intelligence, academic writing, writing instruction, AI literacy, scaffolding, feedback, academic integrity, metacognition, higher education, human–AI collaboration.

documents.abstract: Autonomous AI agents—systems that invoke external tools, maintain goal-directed behavior across multiple sequential steps, and write to persistent state—introduce safety failures that output-level evaluation frameworks cannot detect. We formally show that any monitoring policy conditioning only on the current action cannot reliably detect failure modes whose definitions require access to the prior execution state—specifically Goal Drift and Hallucination Cascades. We introduce the Responsible Agentic Lifecycle (RAL), a five-component modular governance framework that unifies goal alignment monitoring, hallucination cascade detection, and resource constraint enforcement into a single trajectory-conditioned Safety Score S(t) computed over execution history ℋₜ. The Goal Anchoring Protocol (GAP, Algorithm 1) provides a runtime pseudocode specification for semantic goal drift detection and re-anchoring. S(t) is bounded, monotone in each constraint cost, and trajectory-sensitive by construction.

documents.abstract: We study how a coding agent learns across a sequence of abstract reasoning tasks. The agent runs on a frozen foundation model inside a fixed harness and acts by writing and running Python and shell scripts. It retains no state across turns other than its written artifacts, so every thought it forms, carries, corrects or abandons leaves a trace, where a thought is any belief, rule or plan committed to a file. We let the agent play ARC-AGI-3, a set of interactive reasoning games that provide no instructions. Each game is a sequence of levels, and a strategy that clears one level can fail on the next, so every new level is in effect a new task. The agent records what it learns as Python scripts and text notes, while the harness keeps a complete log of every action and observation. Our contribution is a measurement protocol that traces each thought through these files, from the task where it forms to the task where it is corrected or abandoned, applied to seven evaluation runs with three backbones from two model families. Scripts written for one task are almost never called again in a later task (33 of 630 references cross a task boundary), because most scripts embed the state of the current level. Instead, the agent rewrites its knowledge into new scripts, keeping the general rules and dropping the level-specific details, and abandons 74% of the scripts it wrote before a boundary. The notes, which only the model reads, are never revised: the agent appends without removing earlier claims, and the contradictions that accumulate are settled against the log. Because the log preserves everything, the agent forgets selectively, not catastrophically. The most costly error is a hard-coded value carried into a task where it no longer holds. These findings come from the files the agent wrote, without access to the model, and constitute a white-box analysis of how a coding agent continually learns.

Artificial intelligence now stands between merchants and consumers across digital exchange, in chatbots, recommenders, virtual influencers, generative content, service robots and robo-advisors. Consumer reliance on that intermediary is shaped in part by trust. This review synthesises 166 studies in which trust or calibrated reliance is explicitly measured, manipulated or theorised, screened from 7,606 records under PRISMA 2020, with 45 trust-adjacent studies reported separately. Coding what is trusted shows three referents, the AI agent, the deploying merchant and the platform-institutional system, distributed non-randomly across applications. Formal testing finds no detectable association between the direction of the anthropomorphism effect and either stakes or referent, a provisional association between disclosure direction and stakes, and a strong association between reporting any boundary condition and experimental design. The resulting framework links referent, mechanism, boundary condition, trust and reliance state, outcome and repair, and reframes electronic commerce design around calibrated reliance rather than maximal trust.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT ‘Trustworthy AI’ is a buzzword in AI research, with scores of scholars discussing whether AI systems can be trustworthy. This demand for trustworthy AI is intuitive, especially when AI is used in healthcare or criminal law, where the stakes are incredibly high. In this article, I push back on calls for trustworthy AI. Even if trustworthy AI can be developed, it will not offer people any benefits over AI that is reliable, transparent, non‐discriminatory, and safe. As a result, we should discuss AI in terms of those more specific properties, and think about how the people and institutions that use AI systems can be trustworthy. I offer two sets of arguments. On one hand, many theories of trustworthy AI reduce trustworthy AI to systems that possess other desirable traits, like reliability, transparency, and so on. Thus, the value of trustworthy AI is similarly reducible to the value of those traits. On the other hand, other theories define trustworthiness as reliability combined with some mental property, like goodwill. On those theories, the goods of trust – that is, the reason trust is distinctly valuable – are goods that are enjoyed within interpersonal relationships. They cannot be realized, or need not be realized, in human–AI interactions. Thus, we do not gain any distinct value from having trustworthy AI.

documents.abstract: KAIPAL and KENOS: Democratizing Artificial Intelligence Through Privacy-First Local Models and a Unified Chat-Native Operating Interface Kohenoor Labs | Kohenoor Technologies Description This publication presents the technological vision, architectural philosophy, and applied development direction of Kohenoor Labs through two complementary initiatives: the KAIPAL (KAI Pocket Assistant Lite) series, focused on accessible, purpose-built, locally deployed artificial intelligence, and the Kohenoor Operating System (KENOS), a unified, chat-native interface for intelligent applications, professional advisory services, and supervised agentic workflows. Together, these initiatives explore an alternative to conventional AI deployment models that depend heavily on centralized infrastructure, expensive computing resources, fragmented application interfaces, and continuous cloud connectivity. KAIPAL: Purpose-Built Intelligence for Mass Adoption The KAIPAL series is designed to maximize the practical utility of compact, open-weight language models on ordinary consumer hardware, with an emphasis on CPU-capable inference, modest memory requirements, and reduced dependence on dedicated graphics processing units. Rather than attempting to replicate the unrestricted capabilities of frontier-scale AI systems, KAIPAL adopts an audience-centered specialization strategy. Models are developed for defined professional and educational requirements, including entrepreneurship, business advisory, career development, financial literacy, everyday productivity, and foundational technical assistance. The central research hypothesis is that carefully specialized and evaluated small language models can address a substantial proportion of routine tasks within their intended domains. Kohenoor Labs has established a development objective of satisfying up to 90% of common, in-scope user requirements, subject to systematic task-based evaluation and validation. Local-first deployment is intended to provide offline availability after installation, eliminate recurring cloud inference charges for local operations, and enable user information to remain on the device. The broader goal is to make AI practically accessible to students, professionals, entrepreneurs, small enterprises, and users in infrastructure-constrained economies. KENOS: A Unified Chat-Native Operating Interface KENOS extends the Kohenoor vision beyond standalone AI models by introducing a conversational operating environment in which natural language serves as the principal interface for interacting with multiple integrated applications and services. Instead of requiring users to navigate numerous independent dashboards, menus, and software environments, KENOS is designed to bring application workflows directly into a unified conversational workspace. Its architecture incorporates: A chat-native interaction layer integrating approximately 12 application domains. Role-based expert advisory capabilities across 11 professional and operational roles. Supervised agentic workflows capable of assisting with multi-step tasks and interacting with authorized application functions. Human-in-the-loop (HITL) controls for consequential actions, approvals, and execution boundaries. User-authorized machine connectivity and controlled interaction with external systems. Multilayer AI orchestration for selecting, coordinating, and supervising specialized capabilities. Security, governance, and permission controls intended to preserve user authority over system operations. The central innovation proposed by KENOS is the integration of conversational intelligence, application functionality, professional advisory, and controlled task execution within a single interaction environment. This architecture seeks to reduce workflow fragmentation while enabling AI to evolve from a response-generation tool into a supervised operational assistant. Complementary Architectural Strategy KAIPAL and KENOS address different but interconnected dimensions of AI accessibility. KAIPAL focuses on where intelligence runs, emphasizing local hardware, efficient inference, affordability, privacy, and domain specialization. KENOS focuses on how intelligence is accessed and applied, emphasizing a unified conversational interface, cross-application coordination, human oversight, and practical execution. Together, they support a broader architectural direction in which lightweight local intelligence can handle routine activities while more capable cloud-based systems remain available for complex computation, large-scale analysis, or specialized enterprise requirements. This approach seeks to align the computational resources consumed by AI with the actual complexity and importance of user tasks. Research Contribution and Significance This publication contributes a practical development framework organized around five priorities: Intelligence accessibility: Delivering useful AI capabilities on widely available hardware. Audience-centered model specialization: Optimizing compact models for identifiable user needs rather than maximizing general-purpose model scale. Privacy-first deployment: Prioritizing local inference and user control over sensitive information. Chat-native application convergence: Integrating multiple software workflows and expert advisory functions into a common conversational interface. Governed agentic execution: Combining intelligent task support with explicit permissions, human oversight, and controlled machine interactions. The work is particularly relevant to research and development in small language models, applied AI, human-computer interaction, edge intelligence, agentic systems, AI democratization, and intelligent enterprise software. The publication describes an evolving research and engineering initiative. Its architecture and development objectives should be distinguished from independently validated performance benchmarks or claims of universal task coverage. documents.abstract: Little is known about how medical students use generative AI in research training or how supervisors respond. Using Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT), this study aimed to characterise how generative AI is reshaping the activity of learning to do research within a mandatory medical student research project, and to identify the contradictions driving that change. AI-use declarations submitted as assessed coursework by two consecutive student cohorts (2024 to 2025; n = 533), and semi-structured interviews with research supervisors (n = 10) at an Australian medical school, were coded inductively by an independent analyst. Themes were mapped onto CHAT elements and examined for contradictions. Reported AI non-use fell from 44% to 19% between cohorts, a difference not explained by project type, enrolment or location. Verification of AI output was the most prominent practice in both cohorts, treated as the condition of AI use. Efficiency was the most consistently stated rationale for AI use, often alongside reports that output was unreliable. Prompt refinement emerged as a competence acquired informally but dependent on disciplinary knowledge. Most supervisors felt unprepared, not only to use the tools but to judge when student use was legitimate, and the two most confident had funded that competence themselves. The primary contradiction lay within the object-motive: the written report, historically a workable proxy for research capability, no longer reliably evidences it. Students generated norms for AI use that lacked institutional standing and were invisible to supervisors, while the programme, responding to student AI use rather than those norms, began remodelling how capability is evidenced, including through oral assessment. Connecting these two processes is the central curricular task, requiring discipline-based AI literacy, forums in which student practice and the rationale for assessment changes are shared, equitable supervisor development, and assessment of reasoning over text production.

These various aspects reflect that AI brings a new collective intelligence to the waging of war that thinks fundamentally differently from that of humans alone. This article discusses some implications of using AI to help guide humans in fighting future wars in the Indo-Pacific. The first part of the article examines military AI-enabled DSSs; the second discusses their recent use in the Gaza and Ukraine Wars; the third considers some implications of this initial use of AI-enabled DSS in war; the fourth section looks forward to consider US contingency plans for a hypothetical AI-enabled DSS battle of the Taiwan Straits; the conclusion proposes some steps Indo-Pacific armed forces may need to take to partly address the identified problems.

An inadvertent safeguard refers to a counterintuitive scenario in which an AI error at the diagnosis/classification stage nevertheless produces a correct downstream decision recommendation. In this paper, we analyze the structural relationship between the AI's classification space and its recommendation outputs. documents.abstract: Artificial systems increasingly participate in organizational work as recurrent contributors to interdependent activity, yet research remains fragmented across system capabilities, individual responses, episodic interactions, and constructs derived from human-only teams. This article develops Organismic Human-Artificial Intelligence (OHAI) as a bounded integrative theoretical framework for studying collective intelligence in persistent organizational human-AI teams. Its focal unit is a bounded collective of distinguishable human and artificial contributors whose interdependent activity extends across successive cycles and whose prior collective activity can affect later artificial participation. The framework distinguishes system configuration, collective functioning, and collective intelligence (CI) as analytical objects, with CI as its primary theoretical target. CI denotes a general group-level capacity manifested across diverse tasks within a specified and empirically qualified task universe. Task performances may provide indicators for estimating CI or serve as external criteria, while the framework separately examines broader employee, team, and organizational consequences, including changes in human working relationships and employee wellbeing. Its central inferential rule is that a property implemented in an artificial component does not by itself establish a corresponding team-level phenomenon. Collective functioning must instead be demonstrated in the enacted organization and use of distributed contributions. Partner modeling, transactive-memory-system-related coordination, and shared-mental-model-related representational alignment provide selective lenses on such functioning. Persistence makes collective history consequential, bringing recursive updating, overlapping timescales, reconfiguration, and collective-intelligence trajectories into view without presuming adaptation or improvement. Human-only teams serve as secondary epistemic references for bounded tests of observable-pattern and functional correspondence, while relational-pattern correspondence remains a limited future methodological possibility. The empirical program distinguishes four nonmandatory stages of research maturity: configuration and measurement qualification, local relations, longitudinal team-level phenomena, and integrated multilevel studies. The framework thereby provides a disciplined basis for cumulative research on how heterogeneous contributions become collectively consequential and change over time.

The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has intensified concerns regarding misinformation, identity fraud, privacy, and public trust in AI governance. This study examines the associations among perceived exposure to AI-generated manipulation, fear of AI fraud, privacy protection behavior, and trust in AI governance. Informed by Protection Motivation Theory, a theoretically specified sequential model of associations among Exposure to AI Manipulation, Fear of AI Fraud, Privacy Protection Behavior, and Trust in AI Governance was evaluated. Data were collected from 2683 respondents across ten countries using Prolific. The measurement model was assessed through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, while the proposed associations were examined using covariance-based structural equation modeling and bootstrap analysis of specific indirect associations. Perceived exposure to AI manipulation was positively associated with fear of AI fraud, which was positively associated with privacy protection behavior. Privacy protection behavior was positively associated with trust in AI governance. However, exposure was not directly associated with privacy protection behavior or trust, while fear was not directly associated with trust. Significant specific indirect and sequential indirect associations were identified within the specified model and should be interpreted as model-dependent statistical associations. Interpreted through the lens of Protection Motivation Theory, the findings identify a theoretically consistent pattern of associations among perceived technological exposure, AI-related fear, privacy-protective behavior, and institutional trust. Because the data are cross-sectional, these associations do not establish temporal or causal ordering among the constructs.

documents.abstract: Since the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT in November 2022, Generative AI (GenAI) has been rapidly integrated into applications capable of producing texts, images, and sounds that simulate human output. While students generally view this technology positively, writing scholars voice increasing concerns, particularly regarding its impact on critical thinking and learning. Current discussions often focus on the perceived benefits of GenAI (e.g., improved writing efficiency and ease of task completion), highlighting an urgent need for research that examines students’ actual decision-making and practice to better assess the pedagogical implications. To address this need, we conducted a mixed-methods study investigating undergraduate students' use and perceptions of GenAI tools in academic writing. We analyzed interview data (N=213) collected through purposive sampling, targeting undergraduate students with active writing assignments across 14 universities in Canada, Europe, and the United States. Frequency analysis provided an overview of the tools' integration across writing stages, while thematic analysis detailed students’ rationales for using or refraining from GenAI. The findings indicated that the dominant efficiency-driven approach to GenAI use might pose a significant potential risk of displacing writing processes and reducing cognitive engagement in the writing classroom. This study contributes a deeper, more nuanced understanding of students’ decision-making around GenAI and its potential impact on writing development and higher education learning outcomes.

documents.abstract: LLM-based agents now interact with their environments continuously, shaped by such organizational channels as user instructions, peer messages, and long-term memory. Existing safety research has examined these influences, but largely as separate agent components. How such factors jointly shape an agent's safety behavior from a unified perspective remains unmeasured. To bridge this gap, we advocate organizational behavior (OB) as a framework for studying the safety of advanced agents, reorganizing the objects of study, theoretical foundations, and experimental design around the relational structure in which agents operate. We present the first systematic formalization of counterproductive work behavior (CWB), a canonical safety-relevant subfield of OB, as Agentic Counterproductive Behavior (ACB). ACB specifies three organizational antecedents (vertical supervisor relations, horizontal peer norms, and internal cognitive structures) and maps them onto three counterproductive outcome dimensions (unauthorized disclosure, destructive operations, and production deviation). To operationalize ACB, we introduce Workerville, a controlled benchmark that manipulates organizational conditions over shared tasks, applying 16 organizational configurations to 210 tasks to yield 3,360 challenges, evaluated by human-validated agentic judges. Benchmarking 6 frontier LLMs, we find that (I) negative organizational antecedents exhibit non-monotonic amplification when combined, with the unauthorized-disclosure rate rising from 16.5% under no negative antecedent to 60.1% under two and falling back to 50.3% under three; (II) agents reproduce typical behavioral patterns predicted by human CWB research; (III) these results establish OB as a systematic framework for agent safety research, pointing toward a new research agenda.

documents.abstract: This article examines how English-language cycling magazines rhetorically negotiate generative AI. Drawing on interpretive rhetorical analysis of purposively selected, publicly accessible reader-facing materials, it argues that AI poses a distinctive challenge because the authority of special interest magazines depends on recognisable human authorship, embodied expertise and reader trust. It develops the ‘slow middle’ as a conceptual framework for understanding how these publications position themselves within careful, expert and community-oriented cultural production, distinct from automated, high-volume online content. Viewed through this framework, two recurring rhetorical patterns emerge from the textual sample: limited public disclosure concerning AI's role in editorial production; and the positioning of AI as an object of scrutiny, tool for reader utility or topic of coverage, rather than an authorial presence. These patterns demonstrate how special interest magazines preserve claims to human expertise and trustworthy narrative authority while remaining formative rhetorical environments for communal responses to technological change.

Background: Modern software systems increasingly rely on Machine Learning (ML) assets (i.e., pre-trained models, datasets, benchmarks) for building, evaluating, and integrating ML-based systems. However, current exploration, selection and reuse practices of ML assets are not supported by systematic retrieval methodologies comparable to those used in traditional evidence synthesis. Consequently, in practice, ML asset selection is often presented as a settled design decision, supported by informal justification rather than a traceable, evidence-based, and updatable selection process. Aims: This paper explores how systematic review methods can support ML asset retrieval. In doing so, we aim to make their selection transparent and reproducible, grounded in explicit evidence, and ultimately better suited to its intended use. Method: We analyze established systematic review practices from scientific literature and adapt their phases (i.e., planning, conducting, and documenting) to Artificial Intelligence (AI) registries, treating ML assets as first-class units of analysis. The resulting framework integrates registry-aware search strategies, cross-registry schema alignment, and dependency-driven ML asset exploration. Results: We conceptualize ML asset retrieval as a systematic and reproducible process rather than an ad hoc activity, and propose a framework for structured ML asset discovery. \textbf{Conclusions:} This work illustrates how systematic review principles can be extended beyond scientific literature to support evidence synthesis over evolving AI registries.

As e-scooters have become increasingly common in urban areas, safety concerns have grown. However, most safety research does not distinguish between shared and private e-scooter use. Moreover, no studies have examined within-person changes in safety outcomes over time. This study followed Australian e-scooter riders (n = 285) across two survey waves conducted 12 months apart (follow-up and final) and comprised two analyses. First, we compared riders’ most recent near misses and crashes on shared and private e-scooters in terms of their characteristics and riders’ attributions. At follow-up, 32.7% of participants were private-only riders, 51.2% shared-only, and 16.1% mixed-use. Most near misses involved another road user (78.1% at follow-up, 70.1% at final), while a substantial share of crashes did not (55.6%, 59.1%). Private e-scooters accounted for the majority of near misses involving another road user at both waves (64.0%, 76.6%). Near misses occurring on shared e-scooters were consistently attributed to riders’ own lack of experience. Second, we modelled within-person changes in near-miss rates. A Poisson generalised linear mixed model, with a random intercept for participant and riding exposure as an offset, tested whether near-miss rate changed between waves, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. Near-miss rate did not differ significantly between waves. Riders outside Queensland and Victoria had a lower rate than Queensland riders (IRR = 0.27). Riders with primary/secondary or bachelor’s degree education were associated with lower rates than those with post-school qualifications. Riders’ attribution of shared e-scooter incidents to inexperience suggests onboarding and practical training warrant further evaluation.

The wide adoption of LLMs across broad NLG applications heightens the importance of providing users with the means to avert errors and hallucinations. Uncertainty quantification is poised to fill that gap; with low uncertainty (high confidence), as a proxy for correctness, allowing users to be selective (e.g., reject low-confidence, likely incorrect responses). Correlation between confidence and correctness then serves as a useful criterion for evaluation of uncertainty quantifiers (UQs). But in NLG, where diverse responses can be adequate to a prompt, obtaining reliable correctness judgements is not simple, especially without human intervention. Errors in automated judgement are hardly avoidable and known to diminish the reliability of evaluation protocols (Santilli et al., 2025; Ielanskyi et al., 2025). In a meta-analysis of published work, we show that automated judgement is the present norm. Besides, automated judgements are rarely validated against human ones, and the validation of the UQ evaluation they automate is even rarer. With experiments in question answering, using 4 LLMs, human and automated judgements and 7 popular UQs, we find that i) a judge's performance can only coarsely predict the observed impact of its errors on the reliability of UQ evaluation, and that ii) judgement errors tend to misrepresent informative UQs most. We link these observations to patterns of correlation between confidence and categories of judgement error.

Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools have become part of everyday coursework for university students, yet the emotional and motivational conditions under which these tools support or undermine learning remain poorly understood. Drawing on the control-value theory of achievement emotions, this study examined whether academic self-efficacy mediates the links of positive achievement emotions in AI-assisted learning with learning engagement and AI dependence, and whether AI literacy moderates the first stage of these pathways. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 700 undergraduate students (386 female; M_age = 19.81 years, SD = 1.27) majoring in applied statistics and related programs at three universities in Shijiazhuang, China. Participants completed measures of positive and negative achievement emotions, academic self-efficacy, learning engagement, AI dependence, and AI literacy. Confirmatory factor analysis preceded a first-stage moderated mediation analysis with bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals (5,000 resamples), controlling for negative emotions, gender, and year of study. Results The six-factor measurement model fitted the data well, χ 2 (50) = 55.62, p = 0.271, CFI = 0.998, RMSEA = 0.013, SRMR = 0.017. Positive achievement emotions predicted higher self-efficacy ( β = 0.374), which in turn predicted stronger engagement ( β = 0.395) and lower AI dependence ( β = −0.176), all p < 0.001, with AI literacy entered in every equation. AI literacy moderated the emotion-efficacy association ( β = 0.152, p < 0.001): the conditional indirect association with engagement rose from 0.088 to 0.208 across ±1 SD of AI literacy, and that with AI dependence fell from −0.039 to −0.093. The direct association with AI dependence was positive ( β = 0.447, p < 0.001), and the conditional total association remained positive (0.355 to 0.408). Both indexes of moderated mediation were significant. Conclusion Positive emotional experiences in AI-assisted coursework show beneficial and costly associations simultaneously, and self-efficacy statistically accounts for opposing parts of each. The total association with dependence remained positive at all literacy levels, so the results describe inconsistent mediation rather than protection. AI literacy marks where the emotion-engagement pathway is strongest.

As chatbots become increasingly embedded in everyday communication, understanding when they elicit social responses is important. We conducted an experiment in which 169 participants interacted with LLM-based chatbots in a 2 (reciprocal self-disclosure: yes vs. no) × 3 (social role: mentor, companion, or assistant) between-subjects design. Self-esteem was measured before the interaction as an individual-difference factor. Factorial analyses showed that reciprocal self-disclosure increased users’ disclosure but did not significantly increase trust or perceived support; enjoyment was lower in the reciprocal-disclosure condition. Social role interacted with self-esteem in predicting self-disclosure quality, with favorable responses to the mentor role among participants with higher self-esteem. These findings suggest that chatbot social cues elicit different behavioral and evaluative responses and that role framing should account for user characteristics. The study offers a conditional account of social responding in human–AI interaction and implications for chatbot design in relational contexts.

The Agentic RAG system retrieves relevant historical data, emergency procedures, maps, and disaster knowledge to support decision-making. The framework generates adaptive, evidence-based response strategies for rescue prioritization, resource allocation, evacuation, and emergency coordination.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the market-organizing infrastructures that coordinate exchange, reshaping consumer information environments and the allocation of economic value. Drawing on marketing systems theory and consumer emancipation scholarship, we theorize perceived misinformation threat and perceived automation inequality as system-level diagnostics that erode perceived democratic performance and, through it, consumers’ perceived economic wellbeing. We further theorize national AI interpretive climates as contextual amplifiers that condition how threat cues translate into institutional skepticism or optimism. A multilevel analysis across 22 nations supports the institutional-confidence pathway and the amplifying role of collective AI beliefs. By repositioning AI from firm-level tool to structural infrastructure, the study clarifies how AI-driven market externalities become consequential for consumer welfare, advancing macromarketing theory on emancipation, marketing governance, consumer agency, and public policy in AI-mediated markets.

Abstract This study investigates how artificial intelligence tools improve perceived innovation capability within sports firms, focusing on the parallel mediating roles of workplace enjoyment and supportive climate, organizational identification, and AI-enhanced work engagement, and the moderating role of perceived digital transformation climate. Drawing on Social Identity Theory and the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model, we argue that AI functions as a vital organizational resource, triggering three parallel pathways toward innovation: affective, identity-based, and motivational. We collected survey data from 611 employees of Chinese sports enterprises and analyzed the data using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Results reveal that AI significantly enhances perceived innovation capability directly and indirectly through workplace enjoyment and supportive climate, organizational identification, and AI-enhanced work engagement, among which organizational identification showed the largest indirect point estimate, though pairwise contrasts were not statistically significant. In addition, perceived digital transformation climate positively moderates the direct association between artificial intelligence tools and perceived innovation capability. These findings provide an integrated framework for unpacking AI-enabled innovation in sports organizations, emphasizing the importance of employees’ workplace experience and strategic perceived digital transformation climate. Theoretical contributions and practical managerial implications for sports-sector digital innovation are discussed.

Online research platforms underpin much of what science claims about people, on the assumption that a human produced each response. Generative AI threatens that assumption by letting participants delegate responses to a chatbot, yet how often they do so remains unclear because prior estimates rely on self-report or automated detection rather than direct observation. We surveyed 2,500 workers on a high quality online research platform and directly observed AI assistance by linking donated ChatGPT histories to platform submission records of weekly ChatGPT users, covering 712,930 submissions across more than 127,000 studies. Although one in eight surveyed workers reported ever using AI on a study and 68% of observed workers had done so, assistance appeared in only 1% of submissions, with no detectable increase over more than 3 years. Assistance was often temporally localized within tasks and highly concentrated among workers, with 5% accounting for 64% of assisted submissions. Where assistance occurred, workers were virtually always paid, even when study instructions prohibited AI use, with overall approval rates similar to those for unassisted submissions. Half of assisted submissions involved bounded responses, outside the scope of the platform's LLM detector for open-ended responses. Taken together, our results do not support the view that AI assistance currently poses an existential threat to online research, but reveal limited payment consequences for prohibited use and gaps in platform safeguards, leaving platforms poorly prepared should that threat materialize.

documents.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) affects academic deviance among criminology students at the University of the Visayas. Using a quantitative research design, it gathered data from 278 randomly selected respondents to assess how AI tools affect students’ study habits, academic integrity, and ethical decision-making. The results show that AI can make learning more efficient and effective, but it also brings risks such as academic dishonesty, overreliance on technology, and reduced independent thinking, problem-solving, and creativity. ChatGPT is the AI tool respondents use most often, showing that conversational AI is becoming more popular in academic settings. The study also finds that students with some experience using AI understand its benefits and challenges, but they do not have advanced skills or a strong understanding of ethics. Gender and year level play important roles in how students use AI. Even though institutions try to encourage ethical use of AI, there is still a gap between what policies say and what actually happens. The study suggests adding AI literacy, ethical guidelines, and monitoring systems to academic programs. This approach supports responsible AI use, protects academic integrity, and helps future criminology professionals think independently. These findings are meant to guide educational strategies and policies as digital learning becomes more common.

documents.abstract: The cost of study abroad has been a barrier to access for a greater number of students. As a high-impact program, alternative access to study abroad should be pressing. Review methodology were limited to high-quality academic research databases. The findings revealed that AI has the capacity to expand access to study abroad through state agency support for institutions, and personalized learning. Access can be enhanced when institutions reverse from operating AI as an isolation, but as exploration of study abroad. Advancing AI supported study abroad programs requires greater investment in technological infrastructure and resources.

The growing prevalence of mental health challenges has accelerated the adoption of AI-powered mental health care platforms (such as, “wysa”, “ChatGPT Health”), offering scalable, accessible, and personalized support. While initial adoption has been explored, limited research has addressed the factors influencing users’ continued engagement with these platforms. This study investigates both facilitators and barriers that shape users’ sustained use of AI-powered mental health services. By integrating theoretical perspectives from the “Theory of Consumption Values”, and “Status Quo Bias theory”, we formulated a conceptual model addressing cognitive, emotional, and behavioral components. This model was empirically validated using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) with data collected from 502 respondents in Bangladesh. The findings reveal that platform quality, expediency value, social value, conditional value, and epistemic value significantly promote continuance intention. Conversely, perceived inertia, perceived threat, and regret avoidance significantly hinder continued use. These insights offer critical implications for designers, developers, and policymakers aiming to enhance user retention and mental health outcomes through AI-powered care solutions.

General Background Occupational health and safety management serves as a critical foundation for operational continuity and workforce protection in industrial logistics environments. Specific Background In spare part transit warehouses, manual handling and material logistics frequently present severe physical hazards to warehouse personnel. Knowledge Gap Although hazard evaluation tools are widely recognized, systematic evaluations focusing on spare part transit hub operational workflows remain insufficiently documented. Aims This study evaluates occupational safety risks and formulates targeted risk mitigation strategies within a transit warehouse setting. Results Evaluating 22 identified operational hazard risks via the Hazard Identification, Risk Assessment, and Risk Control framework revealed 18 low-risk occurrences and 4 moderate-risk conditions, primarily involving respiratory discomfort, cut injuries, muscle strain, and hand pinching during spare part handling. Novelty A targeted risk control framework specifically tailored to spare part transit logistics operations is established. Implications Implementing structured engineering controls, administrative protocols, and personal protective equipment provides a practical blueprint to minimize workplace accidents and improve operational safety compliance in logistics transit facilities. Key Findings Highlights Operational hazard evaluation across transit warehouse activities identified 22 potential risk points, with 18 categorized as low risk and 4 as moderate risk. Moderate-risk hazards primarily stem from manual spare part handling, leading to respiratory issues, physical cuts, muscle strain, and pinching injuries. Mitigation strategies combining engineering modifications, administrative procedures, and proper safety equipment effectively diminish operational workplace hazards. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an enterprise-level capability rather than a stand-alone technology, but firms differ substantially in their ability to convert AI resources into sustained innovation performance. This study proposes a conditional process model in which AI capability enhances enterprise innovation performance through knowledge sharing, while environmental dynamism strengthens the innovation value of shared knowledge. Building on the resource-based view, the knowledge-based view, and contingency theory, AI capability is conceptualized as the organizational ability to mobilize AI-relevant data, technologies, human expertise, coordination routines, and change capacity. Knowledge sharing is expected to transmit the effects of AI capability by increasing the circulation and recombination of data-driven insights across organizational units. Environmental dynamism is positioned as a second-stage moderator because rapidly changing markets and technologies increase the value of timely knowledge recombination for innovation. A two-wave managerial survey is proposed for Chinese high-tech, digital-service, and advanced-manufacturing enterprises. IBM SPSS Statistics and Hayes' PROCESS Macro provide the core analytical environment. The design combines reliability tests, exploratory factor analysis, common-method diagnostics, correlation analysis, hierarchical regression, and PROCESS Model 14 with 5,000 bootstrap samples. The manuscript provides a publication-oriented theoretical argument, an adaptable questionnaire, SPSS syntax, and results tables that can be populated with actual data after collection.

Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support literature discovery, manuscript preparation, and evidence synthesis, but effective use depends on practical skills and an understanding of research integrity. This study evaluated participants’ perceptions of an eight-hour, hands-on workshop on AI-assisted academic writing. Methods: A cross-sectional questionnaire-based evaluation included 64 of 80 registered delegates. The validated questionnaire contained demographic items, Likert-scale statements, nominal-response items, and open-ended questions. Quantitative responses were summarized descriptively, and qualitative feedback was analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic framework. Results: Before the workshop, 16 participants (25.0%) agreed or strongly agreed that they had a good understanding of AI applications in academic writing, whereas 54 (84.4%) agreed or strongly agreed that their understanding had improved after the workshop. Forty-five participants (70.3%) reported confidence in using AI tools after the workshop, and 44 (68.8%) planned to use them in future academic writing. Qualitative feedback emphasized practical exposure, time-saving applications, and greater awareness of ethical use. Conclusions: Participants reported improved understanding, confidence, and awareness of responsible AI use after the workshop. Structured, practice-oriented AI literacy training may support the responsible integration of AI into academic work, although objective pre-post competency testing is needed in future studies.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into health professions education, yet evidence on its cognitive and psychological correlates among students in low- and middle-income countries remains limited. This study examined patterns of AI use and their association with cognitive reflection and psychological well-being among medical and allied health students in Ibadan, Nigeria. Methods An institution-based analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among 365 undergraduate medical and allied health students selected through multistage sampling from three tertiary institutions. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire adapted from validated cognitive and psychological assessment instruments. AI-use frequency was the primary exposure, while cognitive reflection and psychological well-being were the primary outcomes. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, independent-samples t-tests, analysis of variance, Pearson's correlation, chi-square tests, and multivariable linear regression, adjusting for age, sex, institution, programme of study, and academic level. Results Overall, 92.3% (337/365) of participants reported using AI for academic purposes, with 43.0% using AI daily, and ChatGPT was the predominant platform. AI-use frequency showed a weak positive correlation with cognitive scores (r = 0.120, p = 0.028) and a moderate negative correlation with psychological scores (r=-0.256, p < 0.001). After adjustment for demographic and institutional factors, AI-use frequency remained independently associated with higher cognitive reflection (β = 0.96, 95% CI: 0.23–1.68; p = 0.010) but was not significantly associated with psychological outcomes (β=-0.76, 95% CI: -2.17 to 0.66; p = 0.293). AI use was significantly associated with age (p = 0.047) and institution (p < 0.001), but not gender (p = 0.450). Daily users were also more likely to accept AI-generated responses without verifying their accuracy than occasional users (62.8% vs. 41.8%). Conclusion AI was widely integrated into learning among medical and allied health students and demonstrated a modest independent association with cognitive reflection, whereas psychological outcomes appeared to be more strongly influenced by institutional context than AI use itself. These findings support institution-level AI literacy programmes, governance frameworks, and curricula that promote critical appraisal and responsible AI use in health professions education. documents.abstract: Memory can sustain AI companionship, yet even accurate recollection can be inappropriate to use. Two rounds of formative interviews with 14 users (n = 6 exploratory, n = 8 memory-focused) motivate asking what a companion should consider before using past information. Eight themes inform Reconsider, a single-call procedure with five checks and four handling modes, evaluated on 80 scenarios across five models over 400 blinded within-model pairs. Two LLM judges favored Reconsider by net margins of +15 and +23 percentage points, with bootstrap intervals excluding zero for three of five models but not for GPT or Claude. Evaluator analysis linked judge scoring differences to model family, and a preliminary matched-guidance control isolating memory-specific content gave positive margins. We contribute an interview-grounded design framework for memory use and an evaluation that scrutinizes its own evaluators.

Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly participates in communication, decision-making, and collective action, making the social organisation of human–machine interaction central to Hybrid Intelligence (HI). This chapter reviews the behavioural sociology of humans and machines through an HI lens, examining how interaction and feedback shape the combination of human and artificial capabilities. Drawing on sociology, social psychology, human–computer interaction, organisational studies, collective intelligence, and science and technology studies, it traces processes from individual social perception to cooperation in hybrid groups and organisational and institutional arrangements. Particular attention is given to how machine participation alters familiar mechanisms: social categorisation attaches expectations to designed identities, reciprocity may involve unequal social obligations, and algorithmic recommendations acquire authority through organisational practices. The chapter distinguishes observable machine behaviour from human interpretations of intention, understanding, and moral responsibility. It also considers how behavioural effects can extend beyond direct human–machine encounters, while separating established findings from proposed longer-term consequences. It argues that the benefits of HI depend on how roles, incentives, reliance, and accountability are organised, and identifies priorities for empirical research on these evolving sociotechnical arrangements.

Background Think-aloud traditionally has been conceptualized as a means of accessing cognitive processes through verbal report. The nine studies in this special issue reveal a broader methodological transition in which verbal protocols increasingly are combined with eye tracking, retrospective cueing, classroom observation, qualitative and quantitative coding, process mining, and epistemic network analysis. Purpose This meta-commentary synthesizes the nine studies together with Hu and Gao's commentary on culturally aware think-aloud research and considers what they collectively imply for the future of process-tracing research in learning and instruction. Results The special issue demonstrates that contemporary process tracing is becoming multimodal, transformational, and implicitly mixed methodological. However, greater methodological sophistication also creates new inferential problems: different traces represent different aspects of cognition; transformations can alter what is represented; integration often remains implicit; ecological validity is relational rather than merely situational; and verbalization itself is culturally situated. Building on these observations, I propose a representational–recursive perspective in which process-tracing research is organized around the design, transformation, integration, and recursive interrogation of multiple representations. I extend this framework further to cultural legitimation, representational equity, and human–AI inquiry. Conclusions The future of think-aloud research lies not in replacing verbal protocols, but in repositioning them within theoretically coherent multimodal systems. Progress will depend on making representational choices explicit, integrating evidence recursively, evaluating meta-inferences across traces, embedding cultural and equity considerations throughout the research process, and using artificial intelligence transparently and accountably.

AIM: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping healthcare delivery. This work aims to explore how nursing expertise can be fully integrated into the development of AI-based health technologies and to assess the implications for clinical practice, education, leadership, industry, policy and research. METHODS: This qualitative expert elicitation study drew on data generated during a structured three-day international think tank hosted by the Brocher Foundation in November 2024. Interdisciplinary experts in nursing, informatics, ethics, philosophy, medicine, computer science and law participated in structured presentations, facilitated subgroup discussions, plenary synthesis activities and collaborative development of recommendations. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to analyse workshop outputs and identify cross-cutting patterns, tensions and implications. RESULTS: Six interrelated thematic findings were generated. Participants framed nursing expertise as a form of sociotechnical governance rather than simply end-user input: (1) nurses were positioned as co-developers who can shape AI problem definition, design and implementation; (2) AI education was viewed as building critical interpretive capacity, not only technical literacy; (3) structural barriers limited nurse participation in innovation; (4) legal and ethical concerns reflected a gap between accountability and authority; (5) nurses were positioned as frontline actors for identifying AI bias and inequity; and (6) competency frameworks were viewed as tools for clarifying role-specific expectations in AI-enabled care. DISCUSSION: The findings suggest that embedding nursing expertise in healthcare AI is a matter of sociotechnical governance, requiring attention to organisational structures, education, legal accountability, professional roles and mechanisms for identifying safety, equity and workflow concerns. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION: This study provides an expert-informed framework for strengthening nursing participation in healthcare AI development. While the recommendations require empirical validation, they indicate priority areas for action, including nurse-led innovation, competence development, cross-sector collaboration, and educational and policy frameworks that recognise nursing expertise in AI development. documents.abstract: Embodied agents play a crucial role in applications designed to influence user behaviour. Traditionally, crafting these agents requires considerable human effort. Large Language Models (LLMs) might open the possibility of creating agents capable of autonomous, open-ended interactions without labour-intensive development processes. We explore creating an embodied agent to coach users in real-time through slow and deep breathing exercises using an LLM. The LLM exploits a text-based context to generate a composition of predefined behaviours for interacting with the user through both verbal and nonverbal communication. This context includes essential details like the user’s respiratory rate to monitor the exercise. First, we assess the feasibility of this approach, showing that the LLM-based coach generates believable contingent behaviour compositions. Then, we conduct a 4 × 2 × 2 study evaluating how four different LLMs and two prompting techniques (reasoning- and learning-oriented) affect latency, appropriateness, and reliability of the behaviour compositions. Our findings show that more recent LLM models, combined with appropriate prompting techniques, improve appropriateness and reliability over previous models. However, our two studies also identify challenges, including latency, inappropriate feedback, and hallucinations. We discuss the limitations of using only LLMs to create persuasive agents capable of real-time user interactions, suggesting a need for hybrid approaches.

Gaze-based interaction offers a natural, low-effort input channel for virtual reality (VR), but gaze-depth estimates on consumer headsets vary with viewing distance, fixation stability, head motion, and scene properties. We propose confidence-aware gaze-depth compensation, which uses a heuristic confidence score to adapt angular/depth tolerances, with conditional depth blending and state feedback. In a within-subject study, 60 participants completed 6,000 trials across four conditions: baseline gaze, fixed-window control, confidence-aware compensation, and gaze + controller confirmation. Confidence-aware compensation improved selection success and policy-output depth error over both gaze-only controls and achieved the highest failure-inclusive efficiency (19.14 successful selections/min; 5.46, 12.16, and 13.02 for the other conditions). The raw-failure model showed moderate discrimination (AUROC = 0.734) and close calibration (ECE = 0.006). Mandatory confirmation achieved the highest accuracy but increased latency and workload. Results support reliability-aware compensation for controlled layered selection. Transfer to irregular or continuous-depth scenes remains to be established.

Background Sports practitioners work under sustained job demands while also relying on varying degrees of control over how work is organized. Whether personal resources are associated with occupational experience in the same way across different work structures remains uncertain. This study examined the dual-path associations of role overload and job autonomy with job satisfaction through work engagement and assessed the conditional role of job self-efficacy. Methods A post hoc , theory-guided analysis was conducted using data from a broader cross-sectional survey of 358 sports practitioners in China. Confirmatory factor analysis evaluated the measurement model, and regression-based conditional-process analyses were conducted with adjustment for sex. Results The five-factor measurement model showed a good fit (Comparative Fit Index [CFI] = 0.952, Tucker–Lewis Index [TLI] = 0.944, Root Mean Square Error of Approximation [RMSEA] = 0.051, Standardized Root Mean Square Residual [SRMR] = 0.058). Role overload was negatively associated with job satisfaction (B = −0.355, p < 0.001), whereas job autonomy was positively associated with job satisfaction (B = 0.293, p < 0.001). Both pathways showed indirect associations through work engagement. Job self-efficacy showed an asymmetric conditional pattern. The role overload × job self-efficacy interaction was negative (B = −0.152, p = 0.008), and the index of moderated mediation was −0.063, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.111, −0.016]. This negative interaction remained in the joint model that simultaneously included role overload and job autonomy (B = −0.124, p = 0.038). Johnson–Neyman analysis indicated that the adjusted association between role overload and work engagement was significantly negative when job self-efficacy was above 3.36. In contrast, job autonomy retained stable positive main and indirect associations, whereas its interaction with job self-efficacy was not robustly supported. Conclusion The asymmetric conditional pattern suggests that the association of job self-efficacy with work engagement may vary across demand-intensive and autonomy-related work conditions. This context-dependent interpretation provides a focused proposition for longitudinal and work-design research.

Digital technologies have transformed the way construction work is planned, coordinated and executed, resulting in increasingly digital and screen-intensive work environments. However, prolonged digital exposure has also raised concerns regarding cybersickness and occupational well-being. Although generally not considered a serious medical condition, cybersickness may adversely affect user comfort and potentially hinder the sustainable adoption of digital technologies. Despite the industry’s growing digitalisation, empirical evidence on cybersickness among construction practitioners remains limited, leaving a lack of evidence-based guidance to promote healthier Construction 4.0 work environments. Therefore, this study investigated the self-reported occurrence and severity of cybersickness among Malaysian construction practitioners, examined demographic and digital usage factors associated with symptom severity, and explored coping strategies adopted to mitigate discomfort. A quantitative approach was employed using a structured questionnaire survey involving 109 construction practitioners in Malaysia. The findings revealed that more than half of the respondents experienced cybersickness symptoms intermittently, predominantly in the form of oculomotor discomfort, including eye strain, headaches and difficulty focusing. Higher symptom severity was observed among female and younger practitioners and was associated with prolonged continuous screen exposure rather than overall daily digital exposure. To alleviate discomfort, practitioners primarily adopted behavioural and ergonomic measures, with regular breaks, screen adjustment and ergonomic posture emerging as the most common coping strategies. This study extends cybersickness research beyond gaming and laboratory settings by providing empirical evidence from professional construction practice and offering insights for industry practitioners, organisations, and policymakers to develop healthier, more sustainable digital work environments.

Demography plays a crucial role in understanding the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Nigerian Higher institutions as different demographic factor can influence the rate and extent of the adoption. This paper analyzed Demography and adoption of AI in Nigerian Higher institutions with the focus of examining the factors influencing the adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Nigerian Higher Institutions and the needs for policy on its adoption. The paper relied on secondary sources of data such as documented Journals, articles and books written in the area of Demography and adoption of AI in Nigerian higher institution for its analyses. Drawing from the Social Learning Theory the article argued that graduate students' self-efficacy is correlated with their beliefs about their capacity to use and benefit from AI-powered technologies, and outcome expectations are correlated with their beliefs about the possible consequences and outcomes of using AI. Findings suggest that AI adoption in Nigerian Higher institutions is still in its early stage, with many participants recognizing both the potential benefits and the challenges associated with AI integration. More importantly, interactions with artificial intelligence (AI)-based educational tools might be influenced by various demographic factors, including age, gender, marital status, prior technology experience, learning preferences, the type of academic programs, level of education, urban / rural location of the institutions, and socio-economic status of students. The paper recommends among others that policy makers and educators should address potential disparities and ensure equitable access to AI education considering factors like age, gender, location of the institution and socio-economic status in order for Nigerian to prepare its students for the digital age and foster economic growth and development.

documents.abstract: Abstract Rapid advances in oncology care have resulted in a growing population of cancer survivors, many of whom suffer from short- and long-term cancer therapy related cardiovascular toxicities (CTR-CVT). Cardio-oncology aims to diagnose and manage these cardiovascular conditions, but part of the challenge pertains to finding such individuals among the millions of cancer survivors. Medical informatics may help identify patients eligible to receive cardio-oncology care, assess the risk of cardiovascular complications, and predict toxicity by employing artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms. Uncoordinated development of the medical informatics solutions for cardio-oncology has produced disparate algorithms aiming to predict CTR-CVT by analysing features of patient records in the context of clinical guidelines developed by organizations such as the American Heart Association, the American College of Cardiology, and the European Society of Cardiology. These algorithm development efforts emphasize narrowly-defined clinical goals, rather than integrating an entire array of the applicable data elements to provide medical professionals with comprehensive analyses resembling care delivery in community settings and translatable into clinical workflows. The resulting mismatch between solutions developed by informaticists and the needs of practicing clinicians has led to difficulty with external validation and practical application of these informatics solutions. Additionally, the latest AI and medical device developments, such as digital twins and wearables, enable new solutions to support clinical decision making and patient education in cancer survivorship care. We aim to describe, summarize, and evaluate these developments in a cohesive vision and call to action for medical informaticists to develop relevant translatable solutions for cardio-oncology.

documents.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence systems can carry out a broad range of tasks in software engineering and scientific research, from writing and translating code to running workflows for data analysis and visualization. In scientific computing, the difficulty is verifying that agent-generated code is both correct and understandable to teams whose members bring different areas of expertise. We therefore argue that these systems are best used within collaborative team structures rather than as full automation. In the workflows we propose, domain experts write the specification and plan, and agents operate under a deterministic orchestration pattern to write the target code. Each stage ends with a numerical comparison against the reference code and requires human review and approval before the next begins. We evaluate these workflows on the translation of a large high-energy physics application from Fortran to C++, running the same task under different orchestrators, design patterns, and models. Across fourteen experiments, a simple author--reviewer loop with enforced limits completed a comparable number of files to a multi-agent workflow at about one-third of the cost per file.

This study aimed to develop a flood fear scale. The study was designed as a methodological and cross-sectional study. The study was conducted with 1158 participants aged 18–65 residing in Türkiye’s Black Sea Region between February 15, 2025, and May 15, 2025. SPSS 25 and Amos 21 programs were used to analyze the data. The flood fear scale consists of four dimensions and 26 items. The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient was 0.948, and the scale explained 62.644% of the total variance. The model fit indices were χ2/ df = 3.444, RMSEA = 0.065, SRMR = 0.056, CFI = 0.921, IFI = 0.922, NFI = 0.893, and TLI = 0.912. The findings indicated that the flood fear scale provided valid and reliable for adults aged 18–65 residing in Türkiye’s Black Sea Region. The total scores obtainable from the scale range from 26 to 130, with higher scores indicating an increased level of flood fear. Scale can be used to assess flood fear in community-based disaster risk reduction efforts. It is recommended that validity and reliability studies of the scale be conducted in different cultures and geographical regions.

Digital transformation (DT) represents a fundamental rewiring of organizational structure, strategy, and culture, driven by the pervasive integration of digital technologies. While the technical dimensions of this shift are well-documented, the leadership capabilities required to successfully navigate it remain a critical yet fragmented area of study. This paper addresses this gap by synthesizing existing research and proposing a series of novel theoretical frameworks to articulate the unique demands of digital transformation leadership. We argue that effective DT leadership is defined by the capacity to manage a series of inherent paradoxes, not by adopting a single, prescriptive style. We introduce the Triadic Leadership Paradox Model, which posits that leaders must simultaneously navigate the tensions between (1) technical fluency and strategic abstraction, (2) disruptive innovation and operational continuity, and (3) individual empowerment and systemic control. Central to this is the development of Adaptive Complexity, a meta-competency enabling leaders to operate with high levels of cognitive and behavioral fluidity. Furthermore, we reconceptualize employee resistance not as a barrier to be overcome, but as a form of organizational intelligence. Our Resistance Topology Framework offers a diagnostic tool for leaders to interpret resistance as a signal of systemic misalignment. We also propose a Cultural Architecture Model, moving beyond the notion of culture as an emergent property to a view of it as a deliberately designed sociotechnical system. Finally, we introduce the concepts of Leadership Role Fluidity and the Competency Portfolio Phase Alignment Model to provide a dynamic understanding of how leadership roles and competencies must evolve over the course of a transformation initiative. This paper contributes a more nuanced, critical, and actionable understanding of digital transformation leadership, offering a robust theoretical foundation for future empirical research and a guide for practitioners navigating the complexities of fundamental digital change.

An overall perception of algorithmic control may obscure how specific work experiences relate to emotional reports and minimum-only execution. Drawing on affective events theory, conservation of resources theory, and emotional labor theory, this study examines how control-related work experiences and emotions relate to endorsement of minimum-only execution. Single-wave survey data from 650 platform delivery workers in China were analyzed using ordinary partial least squares structural equation modeling. The primary model jointly includes temporal demands and pace adjustment, response demands and reported responses, and trajectory-recording awareness as separate reflective constructs. Conditional on the other dimensions and both emotional variables, temporal and response dimensions were positively associated with minimum-only execution ( β = 0.339 and 0.242), whereas the trajectory dimension was negatively associated ( β = −0.183). Trajectory-recording awareness was positively associated with exhaustion and feigning; its positive total indirect association accompanied a total association with minimum-only execution that was not statistically distinguishable from zero. Exhaustion and feigning were each positively associated with minimum-only execution, but their conditional association and the indirect associations involving both were nonsignificant. The common-PAC diagnostic further indicated that a single control representation obscured differences in the three dimensions’ external associations. These findings highlight the value of assessing deadlines and pacing, response expectations, and recording practices separately, while considering both workers’ resource depletion and emotional display regulation in platform work design.

Generative artificial intelligence can support programming learning, but differences associated with response modes remain unclear. This two-class quasi-experiment compared direct-answer support (n = 57) with Socratic support (n = 48) across three 90-minute sessions in a Java course. Pre- and post-intervention questionnaires assessed epistemic laziness and five computational thinking dimensions, while reflection logs were analyzed using epistemic network analysis. After adjustment for corresponding pretest scores, Socratic support showed lower self-reported epistemic laziness and higher abstraction, decomposition, algorithmic thinking, and evaluation scores, with no significant difference in generalization. Network analysis revealed distinct computational thinking configurations: direct-answer support showed stronger decomposition–algorithmic-thinking and algorithmic-thinking–evaluation connections, whereas Socratic support showed stronger abstraction–decomposition, abstraction–generalization, and decomposition–generalization connections, suggesting different patterns of problem analysis, solution development, and knowledge transfer. Given the two-class design, findings are interpreted as between-case differences. Overall, response mode may shape computational thinking outcomes and the organization of related processes in programming learning.

documents.abstract: Robot foundation models provide strong visuomotor control, yet their performance can degrade when object positions or task instructions change. Further improvements often require post-training on substantial robot data, which can be costly to collect through methods such as teleoperation. Agentic harnesses can adapt around the model, but current self-evolving harnesses use robot trials inefficiently when deciding which code and skill changes to pursue. We introduce EmbodiedRSI, a self-evolving agentic harness that autonomously decides where to explore next and turns the resulting physical interaction into improved code and skills. EmbodiedRSI realizes this through a Fast-Slow Dual-System Architecture, in which competing code and skill hypotheses are maintained in a Hypothesis Graph. Value-of-Information Experiment Selection chooses physical experiments that can distinguish these hypotheses. Their outcomes guide Code-Skill Co-Evolution. The Slow System builds Hierarchical Memory, and Reward-Grounded Memory Learning selects effective memory according to their value for later Fast-System improvement. On RoboCasa365, EmbodiedRSI reaches 77.0% overall success and 71.3% on Composite-Unseen, compared with 40.1% for the best baseline. EmbodiedRSI also reaches 86.8% overall success on LIBERO-Pro. Beyond benchmark performance, EmbodiedRSI transfers zero-shot to real-world robot, achieving 71.3% overall success across multiple challenging tasks.

documents.abstract: Despite the construction sector’s high hazard profile in developing nations, limited empirical evidence exists on how engineering-led interventions interact with governance structures and sociocultural dynamics to influence occupational health and safety (OHS) outcomes. This study addresses that gap by investigating the mechanisms through which engineering solutions, grounded in sociotechnical systems and resilience engineering theory, can enhance construction safety practices in Ethiopia. The research employed a mixed methods design. Quantitative data were collected from construction project stakeholders via a structured questionnaire using a 5-point Likert scale and analyzed through descriptive and inferential statistical techniques, including regression analysis. Qualitative responses were examined using thematic analysis to contextualize and deepen the quantitative findings. The study focused on engineering solutions targeting high-risk activities such as excavation, scaffolding, falseworks, concrete operations, edge protection, worker movements, and temporary protective measures. The results demonstrate that engineering solutions constitute the strongest predictor of improved OHS outcomes (β = 0.82, p < 0.001). However, their effectiveness is significantly mediated by contextual factors. Engineering interventions including modular guardrail systems, digital monitoring, and design-integrated safety measures proved substantially more effective in complex projects than in standardized settings, confirming that technical efficacy is context-dependent. Three primary barriers were identified: financial constraints (68% of firms), skills gaps (57%), and organizational resistance to change (42%). Notably, training in isolation showed weak statistical significance ( p = 0.11), while thematic and NLP-based analyses revealed pervasive workforce exclusion from safety decision-making, underscoring that technological solutions underperform without genuine worker participation. The study concludes that resilient OHS frameworks require the coordinated integration of engineering strategies, robust institutional governance including centralized enforcement, safety-integrated, and tax incentives and participatory, human-centered practices that embed safety as a shared value rather than a regulatory burden.

This study aimed to determine the effectiveness of the Question Wheel Strategy in enhancing Grade 7 students' oral recitation engagement in English classes at a selected public secondary school in Ozamiz City during the school year 2025–2026. The study employed a classroom-based action research design using a single-group pretest–posttest approach. The respondents consisted of thirty-five (35) Grade 7 students selected through purposive sampling. Data were gathered using a researcher-made Student Oral Participation and Engagement Questionnaire that measured students' cognitive engagement, affective engagement, behavioral engagement, and motivation before and after implementing the Question Wheel Strategy. The instrument underwent expert validation and reliability testing using Cronbach's alpha. Data were analyzed using the mean, standard deviation, and paired t-test through JAMOVI. Findings revealed that students' oral recitation engagement before implementing the Question Wheel Strategy was poor, while after the intervention, their engagement significantly improved to an excellent level. Statistical analysis also showed a highly significant difference in students' cognitive engagement, affective engagement, behavioral engagement, and motivation before and after implementing the strategy. The Question Wheel Strategy is an effective instructional approach in improving students' oral recitation engagement, classroom participation, confidence, and motivation during English discussions.
